Q: Whats a good choice as graphics API for small programs for different systems? A:

I feel like the decision is more about the engine than the API. And drawing a fractal can be done entirely within a fragment shader, so your requirements seem extremely low at the moment. And drawing a fractal doesn't establish a compelling need for coding in C++ against Vulkan or anything heavy-hitting or low-level like that.

If the goal is to do as little work as possible then I like Shadertoy as a platform for doing for small projects like drawing a fractal. It runs in a browser and is using WebGL. You can save your creation and share a link with friends.

If broad support for a small program is your goal then JavaScript + WebGL is a solid API if you don't mind living in a web browser. Sharing with friends and family is as easy as hosting any other web content.

Unity has broad platform support and is a full game engine, meaning it has lots of "batteries included" features so you don't waste time setting up infrastructure. You can build for native desktop or mobile platforms or WebGL.

There are lots of other simple game engines that provide a nice ecosystem for quick one-off development. Godot for example.

Even though you're doing "small programs" I still think OpenGL is a good API if you insist on doing a native build from scratch with no supporting infrastructure. These days, a co-pilot like agent can get you set up with boilerplate.

Vulkan is the definitive good choice for hard-core efficient low-level C-like API with broad platform support. But it's not at all for writing small programs, IMO.

Q: Context initialization failed Spring Maven A:

The error is very explicit (emphasis mine):

Severe: Context initialization failed org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanDefinitionStoreException: IOException parsing XML document from ServletContext resource [/WEB-INF/controller-servlet.xml]; nested exception is java.io.FileNotFoundException: Could not open ServletContext resource [/WEB-INF/controller-servlet.xml]

Move your controller-servlet.xml file to WEB-INF folder.

More info:

Q: Syntax error with exec call in Python A:

It is a character encoding issue. Unless you've explicitly declared character encoding of your Python source code at the top of the file; it is 'ascii' by default on Python 2.

The code that you're trying to execute contains non-ascii quotes:

>>> print b'\xe2\x80\x98Hello World\xe2\x80\x99'.decode('utf-8')
‘Hello World’

To fix it; use ordinary single quotes instead: 'Hello World'.

You can check that block doesn't contain non-ascii characters using decode method: block.decode('ascii') it raises an exception if there are.

A gentle introduction into the topic: The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Absolutely, Positively Must Know About Unicode and Character Sets (No Excuses!) by Joel Spolsky.

Q: How can I create a 3D model file from geometric shapes? A:

I strongly recommend to use some ASCII exchange format there are many out there I usually use these:

  1. *.x DirectX object (it is a C++ source code)

    this one is easiest to implement !!! But there are not many tools that can handle them. If you do not want to spend too much time coding then this is the right choice. Just copy the templates (at the start) from any *.x file to get started.

    here some specs

  2. *.iges common and importable on most CAD/CAM platform (Catia included)

    this one is a bit complicated but for export purposes it is not that bad. It supports Volume operation like +,-,&,^ which are VERY HARD to implement properly but you do not have to use them :)

  3. *.dxf AutoCAD exchange format

    this one is even more complicated then IGES. I do not recommend to use it

  4. *.ac AC3D

    I first saw this one in flight gear.

    here some specs

    at first look it is quite easy but the sub-object implementation is really tricky. Unless you use it you should be fine.

This approach is easily verifiable in note pad or by loading to some 3D model viewer. Chose one that is most suitable for your needs and code save/load function to your Apps internal model class/struct. This way you will be compatible with other software and eliminate incompatibility problems which are native to creating 'almost known' binary formats like 3ds,...

In your case I would use IGES (Initial Graphics Exchange Specification)

For export you do not need to implement all just few basic shapes so it would not be too difficult. I code importers which are much much more complicated. Mine IGES loader class is about 30KB of C++ source code look here for more info

You did not provide any info about your 3D mesh model structure and capabilities

like what primitives you use, are your object simple or in skeleton hierarchy, are you using textures, and more ... so it is impossible to answer

Anyway export often looks like this:

  1. create header and structure of target file format

  2. if the format has any directory structure fill it and write it (IGES)

    for sub-objects do not forget to add transformation matrices ...

  3. write the chunks you need (points list, faces list, normals, ...)

With ASCII formats you can do this inside String variable so you can easily insert into or modify. Do all thing in memory and write the whole thing to file at the end which is fast and also add capability to work with memory instead of files. This is handy if you want to pack many files to single package file like *.pak or send/receive files through IPC or LAN ...

exporting to IGES

you did not provide any info about your 3D mesh internal structure so I can not help with export. There are many ways to export the same way so pick one that is closest to your App 3D mesh representation. For example you can use:

  • point cloud
  • rotation surfaces
  • rectangle (QUAD) surfaces
  • border lines representation (non solid)
  • trim surface and many more ...
